executive_summary: Bank of India presents a low-multiple profitability recovery with strong balance-sheet expansion, but the September quarter exposes funding-mix and provision-quality questions. The discount to book may narrow if returns improve sustainably; the key is separating core spread improvement from treasury income and standard-asset provision reversals.
research_stance: Valuation support with earnings-quality caveats; monitor funding cost, provision reversals and ECL rather than treating cheap P/E as sufficient.

thesis_drivers.title: Balance-sheet growth broadens opportunity
thesis_drivers.evidence: Global advances grew 20.58% and deposits 21.59% YoY in the call; domestic advances grew 17.84%. Faster deposit growth than loans is reassuring, but the liability mix is less favourable than aggregate growth alone suggests.
thesis_drivers.source: September 2026 local financials and latest earnings-call transcript

thesis_drivers.title: Profitability has improved but provisions matter
thesis_drivers.evidence: The call reports standalone PAT of ₹3,202 crore, up 25.32% YoY. Management identified ₹213 crore of standard-asset provision reversals; assess pre-provision operating income and normalised credit costs before annualising the reported profit.
thesis_drivers.source: September 2026 local financials and latest earnings-call transcript

thesis_drivers.title: Cheap book multiple needs a return bridge
thesis_drivers.evidence: The local snapshot shows a P/B of 0.74 x and RoE of 12.4%. A rerating needs sustainable returns and capital discipline, particularly as the ECL transition competes for retained earnings.
thesis_drivers.source: September 2026 local financials and latest earnings-call transcript

industry_context.heading: PSU-bank recovery lens
industry_context.content: Bank of India’s franchise value should be analysed through funding costs, recoveries, credit underwriting and return on capital. Sales/EBITDA/ROCE comparisons with industrial companies are inappropriate.

industry_context.heading: Deposit mix versus deposit growth
industry_context.content: CASA fell to 34.16% from 36.68% in Q1 despite growth in the absolute CASA balance. FCNR deposits and associated lending can expand the balance sheet while diluting NIM; aggregate growth alone does not establish better franchise economics.

industry_context.heading: Macro read-through
industry_context.content: Loan repricing after a rate increase can aid spreads, but deposit competition and investment-book sensitivity are offsets. Higher rates can also expose borrower stress.

cycles.name: Credit / Asset-Quality Cycle
cycles.evidence: Reported GNPA of 1.60% and NNPA of 0.42% indicate a much cleaner current loan book. New loan vintages still need to season, so low current losses do not establish future credit costs.

cycles.name: Valuation Cycle
cycles.evidence: The snapshot P/B of 0.74 x represents a discount to reported book. Whether that discount closes depends on sustainable RoE and adjustments to book value.

cycles.name: NIM / Spread Cycle
cycles.evidence: Global NIM fell to 2.47% from 2.52% in Q1. Management attributed a 5 bp impact to the FCNR programme, making funding and programme mix important to any margin recovery.

cycles.name: Deposit / Liability Cycle
cycles.evidence: Deposits grew 21.59% YoY, ahead of advances at 20.58%, but CASA share declined. Funding availability and funding quality therefore send different signals.

cycles.name: Credit-Growth Cycle
cycles.evidence: Global advances grew 20.58% YoY and domestic advances 17.84%. The current pace is above the unchanged 15–16% full-year guide; FCNR activity and underlying credit demand must be distinguished.

cycles.name: Regulatory / ECL Transition Cycle
cycles.evidence: Management discussed an approximate annual CRAR impact of 0.5 percentage points over four years, subject to board assessment. The final bank-specific model and buffers remain to be confirmed.

valuation.method: Reverse valuation and sustainable-return constraints; point target withheld
valuation.assessment: The snapshot P/B of 0.74 x and P/E of 5.61 x look inexpensive, but reflect lower or less certain sustainable returns than premium peers. Provision reversals and low current credit costs warrant conservative normalisation.

business_economics: The quarter demonstrates volume strength: global loans grew 20.58% and deposits 21.59%. Domestic figures differ, at 17.84% loan growth and 23.29% deposit growth, so not all headline balance-sheet expansion should be valued as identical domestic spread income.

The liability-quality question is sharper than the growth headline. CASA rose about 7% in absolute rupees, but the ratio fell from 36.68% to 34.16% as other deposits expanded faster. The economic test is whether incremental NII compensates for a more expensive mix, not whether deposits increased.
earnings_quality: Global NIM fell 5 bp sequentially to 2.47% even though it improved from 2.41% a year earlier. This mixed comparison is important: year-on-year improvement does not establish that near-term margin pressure is over.

The ₹213 crore standard-asset provision reversal adds to earnings and requires normalization. Local consolidated PAT of ₹3,310 crore differs from the call’s ₹3,202 crore bank profit. Removing the reversal requires an appropriate tax adjustment and a full provision bridge, not a simple direct subtraction from either PAT number.
capital_allocation: CRAR of 17.78% provides current capacity, but management’s estimated recurring capital effect from ECL was explicitly preliminary and subject to Board work. Capital generation must be evaluated after dividends, new RWA growth and the final provisioning rules.

Higher deposit guidance of 16–17%, versus 13–14% in Q1, is a genuine change. Advances guidance remained 15–16%; pursuing more balanced funding can be constructive even if spot loan growth later slows toward the full-year range.
valuation_logic: The dated snapshot P/B is 0.74 x and ROE is 12.4%. A deliberately simplified perpetual-bank identity, P/B=(ROE −g)/(cost of equity −g), using analyst assumptions of 13% cost of equity and 6% long-run growth, would require a steady-state ROE of about 11.2% at that book multiple. This is a diagnostic of the earnings expectations in the price, not a fair value, forecast or calibrated discount rate. A changing growth phase, subsidiary values, adjusted book and surplus capital can materially alter the answer.

A 0.74 x snapshot book multiple is not automatically a margin of safety: the value case depends on protecting normalized ROE after the current credit-cost trough and provision releases. The stylized model’s approximately 11.2% required steady-state ROE is near the 12.4% snapshot ROE, leaving sensitivity to modest return normalization. This comparison is descriptive, not a target or an ECL-adjusted book valuation.
peer_positioning: Union’s higher dated P/B of 1.07 x accompanies higher snapshot ROE of 15.7%, compared with BOI’s 0.74 x and 12.4%. A rerating requires evidence that BOI narrows the sustainable-return gap, not merely that both banks report low current NPAs. Private-bank multiples incorporate different liability and franchise characteristics and should not be imported mechanically.

What proportion of current global deposit growth is rate-sensitive or overseas, and how does it change marginal spreads?
